q: Vegetable oils are hydrogenated to make vegetable ghee using which catalyst?
x: Hydrogen adds to the C=C bonds of the oil over finely divided nickel at about 150–200 °C. Promoted iron is the Haber process catalyst and V₂O₅ the contact process catalyst, the usual mix-ups.

q: Which of these aqueous ions is colourless?
x: Colour needs a d–d transition, so at least one d electron and a vacancy. Sc³⁺ is 3d⁰ and colourless, while Ti³⁺ (3d¹), V³⁺ (3d²) and Cr³⁺ (3d³) are coloured. Counting the 4s electrons as still present for Sc³⁺ is the slip.

q: Aqueous [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ looks purple. The light it mainly absorbs, promoting its single d electron, lies in which region of the visible spectrum?
x: The colour seen is made of the light that is not absorbed; Ti³⁺ absorbs in the yellow-green middle of the spectrum and transmits red and blue, which together look purple. Choosing purple confuses the colour seen with the colour absorbed.

q: Which three metals are strongly ferromagnetic at room temperature?
x: Iron, cobalt and nickel are the ferromagnetic metals: their unpaired d electrons line up in domains and they are strongly attracted to a magnet. Zn has a full 3d subshell and is diamagnetic, so any set with Zn is wrong.

q: Transition metals and their compounds are often good catalysts mainly because they:
o: Show variable oxidation states and can adsorb reactants on their surfaces
x: They can easily gain and lose electrons by changing oxidation state, and their partly filled d orbitals let reactants bond temporarily to the surface, lowering the activation energy. Partly filled, not completely filled, d subshells are the key.

q: The slow reaction S₂O₈²⁻ + 2I⁻ → 2SO₄²⁻ + I₂ is speeded up by adding a little Fe³⁺ (or Fe²⁺). The best explanation is that:
o: Iron ions provide a solid surface on which the reactants adsorb
Fe³⁺ forms a stable complex with S₂O₈²⁻ that removes it
Iron ions increase the activation energy of the reverse reaction only
Fe³⁺ oxidises I⁻ to I₂ and becomes Fe²⁺, which is then oxidised back to Fe³⁺ by S₂O₈²⁻
x: Two negative ions repel each other, so their direct reaction is slow; iron switches between +3 and +2, so each step is between oppositely charged ions and the iron is regenerated. Dissolved ions do not provide a surface, so the adsorption option describes heterogeneous catalysis, not this case.

q: Iron(II) solutions are slowly oxidised by air to iron(III), but Mn²⁺ is not easily oxidised to Mn³⁺. The best explanation is that:
o: Fe²⁺ and Mn²⁺ both have the stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
Mn has fewer electrons than Fe, so it cannot lose a third electron
Fe²⁺ has a completely filled 3d subshell
Fe³⁺ and Mn²⁺ both have the stable half-filled 3d⁵ configuration
x: Fe²⁺ is 3d⁶ and losing one electron gives the half-filled 3d⁵ of Fe³⁺, while Mn²⁺ is already 3d⁵ and loses that stability on going to Mn³⁺ (3d⁴). Assigning 3d⁵ to Fe²⁺ instead of Fe³⁺ is the tempting slip.

q: Most transition metals have much higher melting points than the s-block metals mainly because:
o: They form ionic lattices in the solid state
Their atoms are joined by hydrogen bonds
Both 3d and 4s electrons take part in metallic bonding, making it stronger
Their d subshells are always completely filled
x: Transition metals contribute unpaired d electrons as well as s electrons to the sea of delocalised electrons, and their atoms are small, so the metallic bonding is strong. Metals are not ionic lattices, so that option is wrong.

q: Small atoms such as H, C and N can fit into the spaces of a transition metal lattice. The interstitial compounds formed, such as steel and TiC, are usually:
o: Harder than the pure metal and non-stoichiometric
Softer than the pure metal and strictly stoichiometric
x: The small atoms in the holes stop the metal layers sliding, so the material becomes harder and more brittle, and the amount taken up varies, so the formula is often non-stoichiometric. The ionic option is wrong because the metallic lattice remains.

q: The oxides CrO, Cr₂O₃ and CrO₃ are, respectively:
x: Chromium is +2, +3 and +6 in these oxides; as the oxidation state rises the metal becomes more like a non-metal, so the oxide changes from basic (CrO) to amphoteric (Cr₂O₃) to acidic (CrO₃, which gives chromic acid). Reversing the trend is the usual slip.

q: EDTA⁴⁻ binds a metal ion through two nitrogen atoms and four oxygen atoms. It is therefore a:
x: Six donor atoms (2 N + 4 O) bind one metal ion, so EDTA is hexadentate and forms very stable chelates. Counting only the four carboxylate oxygens gives tetradentate.

q: The IUPAC name of [Ag(NH₃)₂]Cl is:
x: NH₃ is neutral, so silver is +1 to balance one Cl⁻; the ligand is called ammine and the cation is named first, giving diamminesilver(I) chloride. Taking the oxidation state from the number of ligands gives silver(II).

q: In nickel tetracarbonyl, [Ni(CO)₄], the oxidation state of nickel and the geometry of the complex are:
x: CO is a neutral ligand and the complex has no charge, so Ni is 0; four ligands around Ni(0) are arranged tetrahedrally. Taking the oxidation state equal to the number of ligands gives +4.

q: Excess AgNO₃ solution is added to a solution containing 0.010 mol of [Co(NH₃)₅Cl]Cl₂. What mass of AgCl is precipitated? (AgCl = 143.5 g mol⁻¹)
x: Only the two chloride ions outside the coordination sphere are free in solution; the Cl bonded to cobalt is not precipitated. 0.020 mol AgCl × 143.5 = 2.87 g. Counting all three chlorines gives 0.030 mol, 4.31 g.

q: Which of these ligands is bidentate?
x: The oxalate ion bonds to a metal through two oxygen atoms at once, forming a five-membered chelate ring. NH₃, CN⁻ and H₂O each donate one lone pair, so they are monodentate even though H₂O has two lone pairs on the same atom.

q: Fe³⁺ combines with three oxalate ions, C₂O₄²⁻ (a bidentate ligand), to form a complex ion. The charge on the complex ion and the coordination number of iron are:
x: Charge = +3 + 3(−2) = −3, giving [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³⁻; each oxalate uses two donor atoms, so the coordination number is 3 × 2 = 6. Counting ligands instead of donor atoms gives 3.

q: The iron ore magnetite has the formula:
x: Magnetite is Fe₃O₄, a magnetic mixed oxide. Haematite is Fe₂O₃, siderite FeCO₃ and iron pyrites FeS₂; haematite is the usual mix-up.

q: When KMnO₄ acts as an oxidising agent in neutral or weakly alkaline solution, the manganese product and the number of electrons gained per MnO₄⁻ ion are:
x: In neutral or weakly alkaline solution MnO₄⁻ is reduced to a brown precipitate of MnO₂, Mn going from +7 to +4, a gain of 3 electrons. Mn²⁺ with 5 electrons is the change in acidic solution, the most tempting wrong answer.

q: In making potassium permanganate, MnO₂ is fused with KOH in air to give a green compound X; X is then oxidised to the purple compound Y. X and Y, with the oxidation states of Mn, are:
x: 2MnO₂ + 4KOH + O₂ → 2K₂MnO₄ + 2H₂O gives green potassium manganate (Mn +6); oxidising it removes one more electron to give purple KMnO₄ (Mn +7). Swapping the two compounds forgets that the green manganate comes first.

q: Stainless steel resists rusting because, besides iron and a little carbon, it contains about:
x: Chromium forms a thin, self-repairing Cr₂O₃ film on the surface, and nickel adds toughness; the common grade is 18/8 Cr/Ni steel. Copper and zinc are the metals of brass, the tempting slip.

q: In titrations with KMnO₄, the solution is acidified with dilute H₂SO₄ and not with dilute HCl because:
o: HCl would reduce the purple colour of KMnO₄ to green MnO₄²⁻
KMnO₄ would oxidise HCl to chlorine, using up extra permanganate
H₂SO₄ is a stronger oxidising agent than KMnO₄
HCl would precipitate manganese as MnCl₂
x: MnO₄⁻ is strong enough to oxidise Cl⁻ to Cl₂, so with HCl part of the permanganate is wasted and the titre is too high; sulphate is not oxidised. MnCl₂ is soluble, so the precipitation option is wrong.
